title: Building Consistent AI for Contract Review with LegalOn's Daniel Lewis
author: Daniel Lewis

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction

Instead, he reframes automation as a supervised partnership that frees in-house lawyers for judgment, risk prioritisation, technology leadership and business-facing work, with emphasis on technical fluency and knowing when human oversight is essential.

st.t: Contract intelligence: Business coordination exceeds document storage
st.an: Lewis shifts the emphasis from business-wide coordination and obligation intelligence to the narrower unmet need for faster, more confident contract review. He identifies persistent pain despite established CLM products, but does not address cross-department orchestration, ongoing exposure management or whether CLM functions will survive.

kp.k: Legal research incumbents retain substantial data advantages
kp.d: Lewis argues that access to comprehensive legal collections remains a barrier to entry despite increased public availability of case law and its incorporation into major language models. Recalling Ravel, he says court digitization proved too slow for the startup, prompting its Harvard partnership. He qualifies the resulting access gains by questioning comprehensive coverage of subsequent decisions and emphasizing proprietary news and secondary publications; his investment estimates are industry assessments, not a documented cost study.
qs: And one of the things that we fairly quickly discovered is that wave of court digitization was not happening nearly fast enough for a startup like us to survive.
They turn to news. They turn for secondary publications. And none of that is publicly available.
And you’re talking about not just tens of millions of dollars, you’re talking about a lot more than that at this point.

kp.k: Contract lifecycle management left review pain unresolved
kp.d: Lewis reports that conversations with in-house lawyers in 2020 and 2021 repeatedly identified contract review as a leading pain point despite established contract lifecycle management products. This is his account of customer conversations, without a stated sample size, rather than systematic evidence of market-wide dissatisfaction.
qs: in almost every conversation I’d have with an in-house lawyer, contract review came up as one of the top one, two, three pain points that they were describing.
everybody was still having problems once they actually sat down to review a contract, doing that faster, more confidently.

kp.k: Consistency matters separately from accuracy in contract review
kp.d: Lewis argues that unconstrained ChatGPT review can identify different issues and propose different changes across repeated reviews of the same contract. He presents this variability as a business problem even where individual answers are accurate. He also reports seeing an irrelevant statutory reference in a competitor demonstration; this is an anecdote, not a measured model error rate or comparative evaluation.
qs: If you ask it to review a contract, it’ll review it. It’ll give you issues. And then if you ask it to review the same contract again, it’ll give you different issues, some of which will overlap with the first set, some of which are new.
If you ask it to make changes two different times, it’ll make two different changes in different directions.
if you’re a business that cares about knowing what you’ve agreed to, it’s a bug, not a feature.

kp.k: Attorney-authored content grounds issue spotting and proposed revisions
kp.d: Lewis describes LegalOn's approach as using experienced in-house attorneys to specify issues, draft corrective language and supply explanatory practice notes, with AI adapting that language to individual contracts. He claims these playbooks support 80 % plus of daily run-the-business contracts and reduce customers' need to create and maintain their own materials. These are vendor claims; the transcript supplies no independent performance results.
qs: We hire experienced in-house attorneys and they sit down and say, when you’re reviewing a DPA or a services agreement, here’s the hundred plus issues that we think you should look for.
Obviously we’ll be able to then personalize that with AI and adapt it to the contract to fit very precisely into a sentence, match the defined terms, but it’s grounded in trustworthy language.
And it comes with a practice note that explains why we think this matters.
And so it provides folks with a ready to use and trustworthy set of playbooks from day one to review 80 % plus of their daily run the business contracts.

kp.k: Playbook customization accommodates differing legal department maturity
kp.d: Lewis distinguishes small teams without playbooks, organizations with partial coverage and mature teams with extensive internal standards. He says LegalOn supports vendor playbooks, customer playbooks or a combination, using the customer's standards to identify issues and produce redlines. The intended benefit is less repetitive line-by-line work and more attention to difficult negotiation issues and overlooked risks.
qs: Some don’t have any playbooks of their own and they’re a two person team that’s just never had the time to build these things out.
If you’re in between and you’ve got some playbooks, we’re going to help you turn those into AI and you can use our playbooks where you don’t have them.
We’ll spot issues and make red lines based on your playbooks.

kp.k: Reliable redlining requires detailed document engineering
kp.d: Lewis links LegalOn's product philosophy to precision, reliability and continuous improvement. He emphasizes that contract formats, styles, tables and defined language are substantive engineering constraints: mishandling them can undermine revisions even when the legal analysis is useful. This is his account of product requirements and organizational practices rather than comparative evidence about national engineering cultures.
qs: Like the variety of formats that contracts can be structured in and the idiosyncrasies of how like styles are set up and tables and formats.
Like your ability to make a great red line depends on your ability to understand the styles and the formats and the language of the contract in a lot of depth.
And the last piece of it that to me really resonates is this notion around continuous improvement.

kp.k: Customer anecdotes suggest knowledge improvement beyond time savings
kp.d: Lewis reports a health and pharmaceutical customer saying LegalOn's clinical-trial-agreement playbook exposed omissions in its own playbook. He also relays customers' accounts of discovering negotiation ideas, fallback positions and missed details through the assistant. These are customer claims carried by the vendor, with no sample sizes or independently measured outcomes.
qs: And they were like, like by looking at legal on playbook, actually it spotted some issues that we hadn’t built out in our own playbook. And it helped us understand where we had some gaps that we could then fill.

We have other customers who’ve talked about when they use our assistant to interact with a contract that it’s helped them come up with new ideas for negotiating a position or coming up with a fallback option or spotting.

kp.k: Contract review remains augmentation, not unattended automation
kp.d: Lewis explicitly rejects treating contract review as a fully automated process whose output can simply be sent onward without human attention. He locates continuing human responsibility in judgment about negotiation, risk tolerance and how to handle individual issues. His framing is augmentation: automate tedious work to free lawyers for decisions, while acknowledging that the problem remains incompletely solved.
qs: Like there’s no world in which you’re just clicking a button and getting a fully automated contract review that you’re saying, I never need to look at this. I’m just going to send it off.
In some ways, the closer you get to contracts, the more you see the details emerge that you want to put in front of a human for judgment.
Do you even want to negotiate it or what’s your risk tolerance?

kp.k: Sanctions anecdotes underscore continued human verification needs
kp.d: Lewis says his daily alerts continue to surface cases involving lawyers sanctioned for hallucinations and expresses the impression that their volume is increasing. Lambert reports an online list he believes is in the 300s or higher. These are informal observations about sanctions incidents, not measured hallucination rates. Gebauer separately emphasizes human review as foundational; her suggestion that some lawyers expect not to get caught is speculation about motivation.
qs: I have a Google alert set up, so I get…  notifications every day of new cases that mention attorneys being sanctioned for hallucinations.
You’d think the volume would be going down, but it seems to be going up instead.
That the,  message of, know, basically having a human, you know, review and, and, and, know, evaluate just doesn’t seem to have, have gotten through to some people, but yet it’s, it’s clearly.

kp.k: Agents are envisioned across intake, review and stakeholder updates
kp.d: Lewis outlines a workflow in which agents request missing deal information, prepare a matter, apply a relevant playbook, distinguish acceptable changes from non-negotiable or fallback positions, and update business stakeholders. He presents connected multi-step workflows as a development direction, with lawyers retaining review and decision-making roles. His statement that lawyers would welcome AI handling 70 % of tedious work expresses an aspiration, not a measured automation result.
qs: An agent can respond and be like, great, thanks for the request. Here’s what you’re missing. Share that. Now I’m going to tee up this matter and prepare it.
They might get automatic updates along the way as the work is progressing so that they know that their, you know, their red line is going to be handled by the end of the week.
They’d be very glad for AI to take on 70 % of it.
So it’s a variety of agents that are going to be knitted together taking on these kind of multi-step workflows.

kp.k: Agent setup combines embedded know-how with business-specific context
kp.d: Lewis's stated goal is to build reusable process knowledge into agents while letting customers supply their own intake questions, policies and risk preferences. He describes planned conversion of documents, spreadsheets, templates or 10 previously redlined agreements into AI-ready playbooks, followed by clarification and optimization. Moving playbook creation from weeks to minutes is a prospective vendor claim rather than a demonstrated timing study.
qs: Now our goal is to create agents where there’s knowledge and process built in so that folks don’t have to reinvent the wheel every time, but that is personalized to the context of their business and the risk preferences that they have and the policies that they have.

we’re going to build the technology that can take your word document or your spreadsheet or your template or 10 agreements that you’ve readlined in the past, convert those into a playbook that’s designed for AI and designed to work within legal on.
agents that help our customers turn their playbooks or build playbooks for them from a process that can take weeks into something that can take minutes.

kp.k: In-house roles shift toward strategy and technology leadership
kp.d: Lewis predicts that efficiency gains can move in-house teams from reactive review and bottleneck triage toward risk framing, prioritization, process improvement and technology leadership, rather than replacing the department. He illustrates the emerging skills expectation through a senior attorney seeking a GC role who believes she needs experience implementing legal AI and demonstrating business value; Lewis endorses that view, but provides no hiring-market study.
qs: it’s not about replacing the corporate legal department, it’s about reframing their role.
they can then shift to supporting the business in different ways that can be helping better understand risk framing and prioritization.

kp.k: Daily AI use raises expectations and change-management demands
kp.d: Looking over the next few years, Lewis anticipates everyday AI use under intensifying business demands for speed, efficiency and maintained quality. He argues that AI could alter the previous trade-off among adding staff, slowing work and cutting scope. His recommendations are to target costly bottlenecks, think across interconnected processes, develop technology fluency and business orientation, understand limitations and risk appetite, and identify where human oversight is essential. He warns that organizational change is slower than technological capability growth.
qs: one of the biggest changes that everybody’s going to go through over the next few years is the change to using AI every single day.
They have to hire more staff. They have to maybe take more time and things go slower or they have to cut scope. And AI is starting to rewrite that equation.
understand its limitations, understand a company’s risk appetite, knowing when human oversight’s essential.
the pace at which people are changing is slower than the pace at which technology is changing.

kp.d: In the introductory conference recap, Nikki Shaver reports that legal organizations remain relatively early in implementing change: firms may have policies without fully considering enforcement, deployed tools without securing adoption, and evolving approaches to ROI tracking. These are her qualitative conference takeaways, not Lewis's claims or survey findings.
qs: we’re still in the relatively early stages of this change.
firms have policies in place, but perhaps haven’t yet thought about enforcement.
they have solutions in place, but they’re still in the process of driving adoption.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Daniel Lewis presents AI as a means of making contract review more consistent and less repetitive, automating supporting workflows, and shifting in-house lawyers toward strategic work rather than replacing legal departments.
pts.d: Lewis claims that general-purpose ChatGPT contract review produces inconsistent issue lists and revisions, even when outputs are accurate, and can also identify nonexistent or irrelevant legal issues. He presents LegalOn's attorney-authored playbooks, proposed language and practice notes as grounding AI review in trustworthy content, with ready-made coverage for more than 80% of daily business contracts and support for customers' own playbooks. He says customers have used the product to identify gaps in their playbooks, generate negotiation ideas and spot overlooked details. He describes agents that would gather missing intake information, prepare matters, communicate progress, convert existing materials into AI-ready playbooks and support review and redlining; playbook preparation could shrink from weeks to minutes. His claim that lawyers would welcome AI taking on 70% of tedious work is an illustrative statement of appetite, not a measured automation result. He explicitly rejects unattended, fully automated contract review as a current reality. He predicts daily AI use over the next few years, a shift toward strategic advice, risk framing and technology leadership, and a growing need for lawyers to add value beyond answers obtainable directly from software. Separately, he argues that AI has not eliminated legal-research market entry barriers: access to comprehensive current case law and proprietary secondary material remains costly.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Lewis relies on product-building experience, descriptions of LegalOn's design, customer anecdotes and market observations, rather than reported controlled tests or independently measured outcomes.
pts.d: For inconsistent or erroneous review, Lewis describes repeated ChatGPT review behavior and a competitor demonstration that referenced an irrelevant California code provision; he supplies no systematic error-rate study. For grounded review, he explains that experienced in-house attorneys author issue lists, language and guidance. His coverage figure of 80% plus is a vendor claim without a disclosed denominator or validation method. Customer anecdotes include a clinical-trial-agreement reviewer finding gaps in its own playbook and other customers developing negotiation positions or fallback options. He describes time savings as significant without reporting measured hours, sample sizes or comparisons; weeks-to-minutes playbook creation is presented within his agent-workflow vision rather than a documented benchmark. His observation of continuing hallucination-related sanctions comes from Google alerts, not a measured model hallucination rate. For changing leadership skills, he endorses technology implementation as a GC competency, illustrated by an encounter with an aspiring GC, rather than hiring-market data. For persistent research-data barriers, he draws on Ravel's experience, its Harvard digitization partnership and subsequent work at LexisNexis. He reports that major model providers obtained the Harvard collection but acknowledges uncertainty about comprehensive coverage of more recent cases. No quantified evidence is supplied for universal daily adoption or the projected strategic-role shift.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Lewis distinguishes current assisted-review capabilities from developing agent workflows and a next-few-years transition to everyday AI use; human judgment and organisational adaptation remain necessary.
pts.d: At the time of this 2025 interview, Lewis describes ready-made playbooks as available from day one and significant review time savings as already occurring. His agent discussion mixes statements of capability with explicit product goals and future-tense descriptions; he gives no firm delivery dates for the complete workflow. Agents are intended to contain built-in legal knowledge and processes but require customer-specific intake requirements, documents, policies and risk preferences. He says contract review remains unsolved as a completely unattended process: decisions about whether to negotiate, how to handle details and acceptable risk still belong with humans. The shift to daily AI use and greater strategic leadership is forecast over the next few years, under continuing business pressure to improve efficiency without reducing quality. He treats technology-implementation competence as relevant to GC hiring already. Adoption is qualified by the slower pace of human and organisational change relative to technical capability. The research-data argument is also qualified: historical case-law access is partially improved, but he is unsure anyone can vouch for comprehensive coverage after approximately 2019–2021.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The primary affected groups are in-house legal teams, their business stakeholders and legal leaders; a separate claim concerns legal-research vendors and entrants.
pts.d: Lewis's central focus is corporate contract review, including NDAs, MSAs, services agreements, data-processing agreements, office leases and clinical-trial agreements. Small legal teams without time to build playbooks could start with supplied content; mature teams could automate their existing standards; intermediate teams could combine both. Lawyers and other legal-team members would spend less time on repetitive checking, intake and triage, and more on difficult clauses, negotiation, judgment and business priorities. Sales and other internal stakeholders could receive more responsive intake handling and progress updates. Businesses seek faster work and greater capacity at the same or better quality, while current and aspiring GCs face stronger expectations around technology implementation, business orientation and change leadership. Lewis frames this as augmentation rather than replacement and does not quantify job losses or headcount reductions. LegalOn is the software provider in this account, not an alternative legal service provider delivering the legal work. In the research-market discussion, startups and other challengers remain constrained by data acquisition costs and established providers' collections. Lewis does not make a distinct access-to-justice claim.
